reviews.title: Marvel’s Gorgeous New Game Can’t Overcome Its Hulk-Sized Problems
reviews.identity_evidence: Direct registered professional publisher review verified for MARVEL Tōkon: Fighting Souls.
evidence_points: Marvel vs. Capcom is one of the most beloved fighting game series of all time, with a legacy so strong that even after Marvel vs. Capcom: Infinite burned a lot of goodwill, many genre oldheads would probably still sacrifice their firstborn for a new installment. In this way, Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls always had an uphill battle: How could a new Marvel tag fighting game possibly live up to finger-breaking Magneto infinites and legendary tournament moments that people still reference decades later?

While we haven’t had enough time to dig into Marvel Tokon to form a final, definitive opinion on the game — early review codes weren’t sent out to the press — it’s clear that, for better and worse, it’s best to put MvC as far out of mind as possible. Yes, this is a 2D tag fighter with Dr. Doom, Spider-Man, and Storm, but in terms of meat-and-potatoes gameplay specifics, it couldn’t be further from that older series’ ankle-shattering speed.

Marvel Tokon is clearly going for something entirely different, and as such, deserves to be judged on its own merits. The issue is that, even viewed with an open mind, it has a lot of problems as a competitive fighting game. Tokon has a gorgeous art style and a potentially sharp story mode, but between sluggish central gameplay and massive issues on PC, this doesn’t seem like the kind of heroic offering that will have hardcore genre enthusiasts gushing.

That doesn’t detract from the game’s merits, though. Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls is a visual marvel, and Arc System Works (known for Guilty Gear, Dragon Ball FighterZ , and Blazblue) lives up to its own lofty standards. Much of this starts with the characters, which take old school comic designs and apply a subtle but sharp anime sheen (except for Danger, who has been hit with a full Moe beam). Where things really get impressive is how these heroes and villains move, leaving behind Ben-Day dot afterimages, as tasteful old school flourishes combine with over-the-top kamehameha-tier theatrics. Deadpool is a perfect example of how much love went into crafting these characters’ visual identities, unleashing a fourth-wall-shattering barrage of fighting-game references that allude to everything from Super Smash Bros. to Street Fighter: The Movie .

This presentation comes alive in the story mode , which, at least through the limited progress I’ve made in the first chapter, seems quite neat. The basic setup is a familiar one — it’s basically a tournament arc — but award-winning comic writer Kieron Gillen leaves room for small character moments. The premise is that a big-bad, the Champion of the Universe, comes to challenge Earth’s finest fighters for a high-stakes bout: if humanity loses this prize fight, the planet gets destroyed. There are five playable storylines, each centered on a different team of four, with the narrative presented through a mixture of motion comics and literal anime cutscenes. This is admittedly the part of the game I’ve had the least time with — I’ve played about an hour compared to sinking roughly 20 hours into the multiplayer betas — but the mode has quite a bit of promise.

However, if there’s an issue that severely hampers Marvel Tokon both inside and outside the story mode, it’s that the game is currently a mess on Windows PC. While the issues aren’t quite as bad as during the recent beta, this port is very poorly optimized, leading to frame drops. Even with my RTX 3080 graphics card, it is almost impossible to get a fully stable 60 FPS regardless of settings. According to early reports , even users on high-end machines are experiencing unavoidable micro-stutters.

Even if you can run Tokon perfectly on your own setup, these technical issues are so commonplace that you’ll almost certainly run into problems when playing multiplayer. Basically, because of how online play works, if your opponent is getting a low framerate, it will lead to jumpy gameplay even if you share a perfect internet connection. These performance issues seem to be the main reason why Tokon is currently sitting at a dismal 36% user rating on Steam. While there’s been speculation that Sony’s anti-cheat software and forced PlayStation Network integration are why the game is running so poorly on Windows PC compared to PS5, we’ll have to wait and see if PlayStation addresses these integrations.

However, even if you’re playing on console, Marvel Tokon is a sluggish fighting game that feels at war with itself, attempting to appeal to newcomers and genre veterans without fully satisfying either. Nearly everything about its core movement is slow, seemingly so that beginners won’t be “overwhelmed” compared to the quicker-paced games Arc System Works used to make, like Blazblue or even Dragon Ball FighterZ . Sprinting and air dashes aren’t particularly fast, and attacks feel quite lethargic, with a good amount of startup and recovery. At the same time, this is a four-versus-four tag fighter that lets players fill the screen with projectiles and massive hitboxes, something that high-level competitors are already using to set up criminal sequences and wonky mix-ups.

Basically, while elements of the game feel similar to something like Granblue Fantasy Versus , which is very beginner-focused, this is also a tag fighter, which tends to allow for high-power-level nonsense. The result is awkward, as it has neither the more tactical pace found in ground-based games nor the speed and skill expression of older air-dash-focused fighters. Those who have bounced off more recent Arc System Works-published titles like Guilty Gear Strive or DNF Duel will likely have similar complaints here.

Another issue is that it seems a bit too easy to perform overbearing pressure sequences that give your opponent little room to interact. While there is a mechanic called “Crossover” where the defender can spend assist meter to push their foe back, the attacker can react with their own Crossover (which I’m sure high-level players will be able to do consistently quite soon) to keep up the aggression. Hopefully, players will find ways around this, perhaps by using a universal armored move called Assemble Counter, but at least right now it seems like skilled play may involve sitting in block for long periods while waiting to get your turn back, which isn’t particularly exciting.

Arc System Works can do just about anything, including convincing me to pick up a Marvel-themed 2D anime fighter. Not that I've got anything particularly against either of those things. But as someone who grew up firmly in the 3D fighting game scene (and continues to dwell there) and traditionally doesn't care much for superheroes beyond Spider-Man, Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls should be a hard sell for someone like me.

And yet Arc System Works has utterly enamoured me to its riff on both the Marvel universe and tag fighters, having me grumble significantly less about anti-airs and jump cancels than I traditionally would. Its low skill floor and high skill ceiling leaves tons of room for expression, from casual autocombo mashers to professionals who can hit you with a two-touch death combo if you're not careful.

Whereas most tag fighters are a conservative 2v2 or 3v3 battle, Marvel Tōkon pits a whopping four characters against each other. That would be downright terrifying by usual tag fighter rules—learning two characters has put more than enough folks off the likes of Tekken Tag Tournament and 2XKO—but Tōkon grounds its larger teams by giving all characters a shared health bar.

It means you can essentially play Tōkon as a 1v1 with the odd assist here and there, while letting you go ham with a full team if you want to. But the game doesn't give you access to all four outright. Instead, you'll start with two characters, continuing to build out your team throughout the match through things like stage breaks, wall splats, and… well, losing the round. It folds in an element of strategy that I really like and stops Tōkon from feeling like a total snowball fest.

Its roster of characters is genuinely stellar, too. Each fighter is already loosely grouped up into a team—you've got the classic Avengers with Captain America, Iron Man, Black Panther, and Hulk. My personal favourite is the Samurai Outlaws comp made up of Ghost Rider (I am now a little obsessed with Robbie Reyes), Blade, Deadpool, and Loki.

Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls is the prettiest fighting game in years and a rousing comeback for the Marvel tag fighter. A wonderfully diverse roster of superheroes and supervillains is realized not just with reverence to their comic boots roots, but also with a fresh Japan-inspired twist. It's somehow a chaotic yet still approachable 4v4 fighter not short on style or substance.

Every match in Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls feels like it could be ripped fresh from the pages of a comic book in how it builds a tight narrative of clashing superheroes and supervillains. While it may begin as a traditional 2v2 bout, the end of a combo at the edge of a screen smashes the opponent out of one panel and across the stage when another hero suddenly joins, turning this into a 3v2, while each subsequent loss sees another hero jumping into the fray until it culminates in an epic 4v4 showdown. These are the largest teams of any tag fighter to date, and no franchise is better suited than Marvel, which gave birth to this sub-genre back in the '90s with X-Men vs. Street Fighter – which eventually morphed into the iconic Marvel vs Capcom .

The difference, however, is that this latest Marvel fighter has changed hands to another Japanese studio, and in the hands of Arc System Works, it's a much-needed course-correct following the nadir of Marvel vs Capcom: Infinite . Without the heavy hand of the Marvel Cinematic Universe influencing story and art direction, Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls instead goes back to its comic book with an anime twist that naturally fits the studio behind stylish anime fighters like Guilty Gear Strive and Dragon Ball FighterZ like an Infinity Gauntlet.
Release date: August 6, 2026 Platform(s): PC, PS5 Developer: Arc System Works Publisher: Sony Interactive Entertainment

Every frame of animation in Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls is just gorgeous to behold. You're so convinced that it's 2D animation of the highest caliber until you launch an opponent or execute a screen-filling super skill that shows these character models from a different camera angle. It's a style that Arc System Works has already perfected with its past titles, but also one that it wisely doesn't overly rely on.

To Sony and Marvel's credit, there's no attempt to shoehorn in a half-baked cinematic story mode with the existing assets. Instead, it leans into its origins by literally having episodes that unfold as comic books. And I don't mean the basic, visual novel-style bookends of Street Fighter 6 's arcade mode.
